skills.when_to_use: The question asks for a judgment whose evidence is distributed across at least two of the supplied videos — e.g., which video shows a given visible activity or object, how the same or related visual content differs or corresponds between videos, or a combined property that no single video can establish — and visual observation of the video content, not just IDs, durations, option wording, or counts, is needed. Applicable whenever coordinating the full evidence workflow for such a question, including cases where fine-grained cross-video visual detail or ordering must be compared directly.
skills.strategy:
Goal: obtain and combine visual evidence from multiple videos to answer the complete question. Work with the exact video IDs and durations supplied; never treat metadata as the answer.

Step 1 — Decompose and check History. Read the complete question and list, per video, the distinct visual facts needed (activities, objects, settings, timing of visible events, attributes). Check public History (prior per-video analyses and joint-watch results): any fact already returned with a clear video ID and sufficient detail is retained evidence; do not re-request it. If History already covers every needed fact from all relevant videos, skip to answering.

Step 2 — Separate per-video facts. For facts that a single video can establish on its own, use analyze_videos. Write each local instruction as self-contained: name exactly what to look for and what to report (visible actions/attributes, approximate timing, what is absent), without referencing the full question, other videos, cross-video comparisons, or computed mappings. Select all videos whose facts are still missing. Keep instructions within the shared character limits.

Step 3 — Joint visual comparison. When the question itself hinges on a cross-video relationship that separate summaries cannot settle — e.g., whether the same person/object/motion/appearance appears in two videos, a fine-grained difference, correspondence, or temporal ordering of brief events — use watch_videos on at least two distinct relevant videos. The instruction string is the entire prompt to the visual model: name the selected video IDs, describe exactly which visible relationship or detail to compare, and request a concise natural-language comparison. Choose one clip per video with start/end seconds inside that video's duration; use durations and any timing facts from History to target the relevant segments. Remember all selected clips share one 512-frame capacity: broader clips reveal more of the sequence but sample more sparsely, so prefer narrow clips around known or likely event times when the target is brief or fine-grained, and longer clips when overall sequence or context matters. Do not ask the visual model to choose the final answer.

Step 4 — Conditional follow-ups. After results return: (a) if a needed fact is missing, vague, or contradicts another result, issue a follow-up analyze_videos instruction for that video, embedding the already-returned facts it must refine or reconcile; (b) if the disagreement is a fine visual detail or ordering that per-video agents cannot compare, issue a targeted watch_videos on the narrowest relevant clips; (c) if a joint result is too sparse or inconclusive about a brief detail, re-run watch_videos with shorter clips centered on the candidate moments. Stop refining when the returned evidence already determines the answer or when no permitted action could change the judgment — do not spend steps on redundant checks.

Step 5 — Answer. Submit answer with a concise evidence-based reason that cites which video contributed which observed fact and notes any material uncertainty. Match the requested answer representation from the question; if options are present, return only the selected option label (or explicitly requested option text). If some evidence remains incomplete after useful checks are exhausted, still commit to the best-supported judgment rather than discussing the gap.
